newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gencor Zambia mine move surprises analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gencor Zambia mine move surprises analysts.

text.p: Gencor Ltd's surprising decision to pull out of a consortium to develop Zambia's Konkola Deep copper mine may mean the South African mining giant did not want to spend huge amounts of cash on an asset it would not manage, analysts said on Thursday.

Analysts said they were surprised at Gencor's announcement early on Thursday that it has withdrawn from the consortium comprising Gencor (30 percent), Anglo American Corp of South Africa subsidiary Zambia Copper Investments Ltd (ZCI) (40 percent) and Falconbridge Ltd (30 percent).
"After careful study, Gencor concluded that in view of all the current circumstances the project would probably not meet its investment criteria," Gencor said.

Gencor is the second company in less than a year to pull out of the consortium. Last July, Australia's Western Mining Corp pulled out of the consortium, saying the Konkola project did not meet the firm's criteria.
"Konkola is a robust project but it needs a lot of money
upfront and that can scare people," said John Clemmow, an analyst at Investec Securities.

"I would suspect that Gencor is saying that the numbers do not add up, it is possible that they didn't want to commit that size of funds for something they wouldn't manage. Because I think Anglo American would have been the senior partner," Clemmow said.

The consortium said earlier this year it would cost between $700 million to $800 million to develop the Konkola Deep mine -- seen as crucial to the country's mining industry hard hit by declining copper production and low gold prices.
The mainstay of the copper industry at present, the Nchanga open-pit mine, is expected to run out of ore by 2000.
Metals analyst Stephen Briggs of stockbrokers EW Balderson said it was not normal for South Africa's two biggest mining houses to work together on a project.
"It is not normal historically for the two biggest mining groups in South Africa to go into joint ventures.
"I don't think it will necessarily put Anglo off unless something has been discovered which really suggested it is going to be problematic mining and therefore high cost," Briggs said.
Anglo's ZCI said that it and Falconbridge would continue with the feasibility study and ongoing negotiations with the Zambian government and Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd.
"The possibility of inviting other companies to join ZCI and Falconbridge in the consortium will be considered in due course," ZCI said.
Briggs said the participation of foreign companies was crucial to Konkola Deep's development.
"Clearly, ZCCM and Zambia would never in a million years develop Konkola Deep on their own," Briggs added.

ZCCM is in the throes of privatisation. Last month the government invited six bidders for the final negotiations on the sale of ZCCM assets, including Konkola Deep which had been lumped in one tranche with the Mufulira smelter.
Zambian officials indicated earlier this month that they wanted some of the ZCCM packages up for sale to be renegotiated -- including Konkola Deep -- but ZCCM said the process would not be delayed.
The unidentified resource at the Konkola Deep mine contains 340 million tonnes at 3.8 percent copper content.
The project envisages mining the ore body to a depth of around 1,740 metres to produce around six million tonnes of ore a year.
Planned output would be around 180,000 tonnes of finished copper a year which could increase to 340,000 tonnes.
